title: Checkpoint: Countries and the World
objective: After this level you can explain how countries cooperate and settle disputes.
summary: The 1959 Antarctic Treaty froze claims and kept a continent for peace and science. Countries talk through diplomats, promise by treaty and settle disputes in courts.

cards.headline: A whole continent is run by a treaty signed in 1959.
cards.body: On 1 December 1959, twelve countries whose scientists had taken part in the International Geophysical Year (1957–58) signed the Antarctic Treaty in Washington. It came into force in 1961 and now has 58 parties. It's this chapter in a single document.

cards.headline: Sovereignty, parked
cards.body: Seven of the signers, including Argentina, Chile and the UK, had claimed parts of Antarctica, and some claims overlapped. The treaty didn't decide who was right. Article IV neither denies nor supports the claims, and allows no new or enlarged ones while the treaty is in force. Level 81's final say, put on hold by agreement.

cards.headline: Peace, science and open doors
cards.body: Article I says Antarctica shall be used for peaceful purposes only: no military bases, no nuclear explosions. Scientists keep the freedom to investigate and must share their results. And trust is backed by checking: every station is open to inspection at all times. Unlike Level 82's embassy door, nothing here stays shut.

mascot.line: Ten levels on how countries get along, and a whole continent to prove it can work.

items.label: How do countries talk?
points: Their premises can't be entered without consent

items.label: How do they make promises?
points: Treaties bind once a state ratifies
Agreements must be kept in good faith

items.label: How do they settle disputes?
points: The ICJ hears states that consent
The ICC tries individuals for the gravest crimes

cards.headline: Chapter 9 complete
learned: The Antarctic Treaty froze claims by agreement
Antarctica: peace, science and open inspection
Countries talk through diplomats and promise by treaty

questions.prompt: What does Article IV of the Antarctic Treaty do with territorial claims?

options.label: It divides the continent equally among signers
options.rationale: It doesn't divide anything; it freezes claims.

options.label: It freezes them: no new or enlarged claims
It hands the whole continent to the UN
options.rationale: The UN has no such role in the treaty.

options.label: It cancels every existing claim for good
options.rationale: It neither denies nor supports the claims.

questions.explanation: Article IV neither denies nor supports existing claims and allows no new or enlarged ones while the treaty is in force.

questions.prompt: Why are all Antarctic stations open to inspection at all times?

options.label: So tourists can visit any base they like
options.rationale: Inspection is about compliance, not tourism.

options.label: Because stations are owned by the UN
Because no scientist may work there alone
So countries can check the treaty is kept

questions.explanation: Article VII opens every station to inspection at all times, to check that the treaty's rules, like peaceful use only, are observed.

questions.prompt: Countries and the World checkpoint: which list puts these agreements in order, oldest first?

options.label: Westphalia → Kadesh → UN Charter → Antarctic Treaty
options.rationale: Kadesh (around 1269 BC) is far older than Westphalia (1648).

options.label: Kadesh → UN Charter → Westphalia → Antarctic Treaty
options.rationale: Westphalia (1648) came long before the UN Charter (1945).

options.label: Kadesh → Westphalia → UN Charter → Antarctic Treaty
Kadesh → Westphalia → Antarctic Treaty → UN Charter
options.rationale: The UN Charter (1945) came before the Antarctic Treaty (1959).

questions.explanation: Kadesh (around 1269 BC), Westphalia (1648), the UN Charter (1945), the Antarctic Treaty (1959).

questions.prompt: Back to Level 87: who can be tried at the ICC, and who are the parties at the ICJ?

options.label: ICC: individuals. ICJ: states only
ICC: states only. ICJ: individuals
Both courts hear only individuals
Both courts hear only states

questions.explanation: The ICC tries individuals for the gravest crimes; only states may be parties at the ICJ.

questions.prompt: Back to Level 88: who of these is a refugee under the 1951 Convention?

options.label: Someone who moves abroad for a better-paid job
Someone who fled persecution to another country
Someone who fled danger but stayed inside their country
options.rationale: They're displaced but haven't left their country.

options.label: Someone on holiday who loses their passport
options.rationale: A lost passport doesn't make someone a refugee.

questions.explanation: A refugee is outside their own country because of a well-founded fear of persecution; people displaced inside their country aren't refugees in law.
